details:
Project Details — Mars 30

Mars 30: A Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-based, 2D educational survival strategy game designed to introduce children ages 7–12 to the challenges of managing a Mars outpost.

How It Works

Players become NAS, a junior astronaut assigned to restore a damaged outpost left behind by a previous mission. Guided by GIL, an onboard AI assistant character, players must repair essential facilities, manage oxygen, water, food, and energy, grow crops, and protect the crew from environmental hazards.

The mission lasts 30 Martian days. Each day, players choose tasks, manage limited resources, and make decisions that affect the following days. Dust storms can reduce solar power, damaged equipment can disrupt life support, and radiation events may require the crew to seek shelter.

At the end of the mission, the game evaluates whether the restored outpost could sustain its crew for another 150 days.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Mars 30 helps children understand complex space science through interactive decision-making rather than memorization.

The game encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, resource management, and long-term planning. It demonstrates how astronauts must balance competing needs and how even small decisions can affect mission success.

Our goal is to make space exploration more accessible, engaging, and understandable for young learners.

Technology and NASA Resources

Mars 30 was developed using:

  • React, TypeScript, and Vite for the web application and interface.
  • Phaser 3 for the interactive 2D game environment.
  • CSS for interface styling.

The game draws on NASA research and data from four sources:

  • DONKI: Space weather and solar activity.
  • MEDA: Martian environmental observations.
  • RAD: Radiation measurements from the Curiosity rover.
  • MOXIE: Oxygen production experiments on Mars.

These resources inform the game's environmental hazards, radiation protection, and life-support concepts. Gameplay mechanics are simplified to remain understandable for children.

Creativity and Innovation

Unlike traditional space education materials that primarily present information, Mars 30 allows children to experience the consequences of their decisions.

Its blocky, colorful 2D art style draws inspiration from familiar games such as Minecraft and Roblox, making the experience approachable for younger players.

Instead of building an outpost from scratch, players restore an abandoned facility while working with limited resources. This creates meaningful challenges where repairing one system may require sacrificing time or resources needed elsewhere.

Design Considerations

Our team prioritized scientific relevance, accessibility, engaging gameplay, and a manageable learning curve.

We designed the game to run directly in a web browser without requiring installation or an account. We also focused on clear visual feedback, simple controls, age-appropriate explanations, and gameplay decisions that demonstrate real engineering trade-offs.

Mars 30 aims to turn space science into an experience where children learn by exploring, deciding, and discovering the consequences of their choices.
